Text: What red flag did you have right before a job offer that you wish you had heeded? Truth be told, I have a penchant for ignoring red flags, especially if there's the slightest promise of getting ahead. This is something I've had to actively work on over the years, but even with that conscious effort, I've still stumbled. Case in point: during my brief stint as a media consultant. Fresh out of university, starry-eyed and eager to "make a name for myself," I was offered what seemed like a dream gig at a burgeoning PR firm. The job promised exposure, a competitive salary, and the opportunity to work with high-profile clients. The interview process had been gruelling, a multi-stage marathon of personality tests, case studies, and panel discussions. I thought I'd aced them all. During my final interview, however, there was a moment, a tiny discordant note that I should've paid more attention to, but which I, in my eagerness, brushed aside. The CEO, a charismatic but undeniably arrogant man, spent a significant portion of the interview talking about the "competitive nature" of the industry and how "mediocrity wouldn't be tolerated". He also made a point of emphasizing the long hours and demanding workload. My red flag was his constant references to 'teamwork' yet he continually used the words ‘I’ and ‘me’ in every sentence. Now, in retrospect, that should have been a screaming siren. It spoke of a top-down structure, a lack of appreciation for employees, and an environment where individual ambition would be prized above all else. Yet, I was so caught up in the aura of the office, the promise of prestige, and the potential payday that I chose to ignore it. As I sat there, nodding and smiling, I convinced myself that I was tough enough, driven enough, to thrive in such a cutthroat world and that all of this ‘teamwork’ talk was simply industry lingo. Within a few weeks of starting that job, it was clear that my initial instincts had been correct. The environment turned out to be as toxic as I had feared. The long hours, the unrelenting pressure, and the constant backstabbing took a heavy toll. The CEO's leadership style was, to put it mildly, dictatorial. I was miserable. I ended up resigning after just four months, wiser, definitely poorer, and with a healthy dose of cynicism. These days, I'm more attuned to those subtle warning signs. I've learned to trust my gut, which is to say, I ask more probing questions and do more background research. It's a lesson I had to learn the hard way, but I’m better for it, I suppose.

Text: Why do women *hate* nerdy men? When I was coming into my teens I was a proper nerd. I was obsessed with Japanese anime, foreign films, the 60s and the psychedelic rock of the period. When I wasn't writing my pompous and psudo-artsy short stories I was spending hours behind the PlayStation and computer playing video games. When I wasn't watching late night soft-core porn on Cinemax I was delighting in clips from the Classical Arts Showcase channel. I would rant and vent about how awful the girls in my school were to the girls in my school. I would find solace in the public library where I scoured the building looking for that quiet, introverted pretty young girl(s) from an all girls school and would proceed to sit next to her(them) without asking permission and then I would gush about my unfinished surreal novel about a country boy in my class having trouble deciphering dreams from reality and vice versa. These girls would find me mildly amusing and interesting but I didn't seem to understand that 'Sorry my parents don't allow me to give out our phone number is actually a diplomatic way of saying no. (This was before cell phones were a thing.) Yes I was a nerd. A big nerd. I still am. However girls didn't hate the nerd in me. What they didn't like was that: Those behaviors had a hint of the creepy about them. It felt as though if one dared to stare into my eyes, the eyes of your classic “nerd,” they might get a glimpse into a soul that had been through the ninth circle of hell. Nerds can be annoying but harmless. As an awkward adolescent with no friends and a bad case of acne, I couldn't understand what girls wanted. I thought my extensive knowledge of the Lord of the Rings trilogy and my encyclopedic understanding of the works of David Lynch and Antonioni were enough to woo any one of those, so-called, beautiful girls. They were not. And they never would be. The girls didn’t *hate* me. They hated the signs of possible narcissists, self-centred a**holes, crybabies and sociopaths. Not that I was any of the above it’s just that those are the type of men girls really *hate* and even fear. Not nerds so much.

Text: Whom did you feel bad for in high school? As a skinny, awkward teenager, high school felt like navigating a minefield of social landmines. I wasn't particularly popular, nor was I a pariah. I existed in a sort of purgatorial middle ground, flitting between cliques and trying to find my place in the convoluted hierarchy that is adolescence. Truthfully, I felt bad for almost everyone at some point. The jocks, perpetually worried about their image and performance; the preps, suffocated by familial expectations and social pressures; the misfits, ostracized for their differences – each carried a burden of their own making, or one imposed upon them. But the person I felt the most sympathy for, and the one who's story sticks with me still, was a girl named Sarah. She was a year my senior, and stunningly beautiful. Bright, witty, and possessing a sharp intelligence, Sarah should have been the queen of the school. Instead, she was quietly battling a debilitating eating disorder, hidden beneath layers of makeup and forced smiles.

Text: Has your friend ever saved your life? Not in any literal sense, thankfully. My friends have frequently saved me from various degrees of embarrassment, which, let’s be honest, can be just as mortifying and sometimes more difficult to bounce back from than a near-death experience. One friend, let’s call him Kevin because, well, that’s his name, has a particular knack for rescuing me from social catastrophes. Kevin possesses an almost preternatural ability to sense when a social interaction is on the verge of imploding. He has the uncanny ability to interject with a timely joke, a well-placed distraction, or a sudden, urgent summons that allows me to escape a conversational quagmire unscathed.  There was that time I found myself trapped in a conversation at a party, cornered by this woman who was relentlessly talking about her cats. I am, as a matter of fact, not a cat person. After an uninterrupted half-hour of detailed descriptions of flea infestations and the peculiar habits of her feline companions, I could feel my sanity slipping. I was desperately searching for a non-offensive exit strategy, but the cat lady was like a psychological terminator. I was completely trapped. Just when I thought I would be subjected to another hour of unsolicited cat anecdotes, Kevin swooped in, feigning a panicked expression, and loudly announced, “Elijah! I need your help immediately! Remember that thing we were supposed to do? It’s now or never!” And that, folks, was my miraculous escape.  Then there was the incident with the karaoke. After a couple of adult beverages, I, regrettably, volunteered to perform. The song was some horrendous, power ballad. My voice is not what I’d consider a gift from the muses, and my rendition was disastrous. As bad was it could be. I butchered every single note. In fact, I was so bad, I was quickly becoming that spectacle everyone remembers and regrets the next morning. Seeing my impending humiliation, Kevin, without a moment’s hesitation, jumped up on stage and started doing the most outlandish, over-the-top dance moves whilst simultaneously grabbing the microphone. He began to sing along out of key even louder than I, effectively drawing all the attention away from my audible malpractice. It was the most selfless act of friendship I’ve ever witnessed. He saved me from myself, and the memory of what would have been a lifetime karaoke shame was averted.  So no, my friends have never saved my life from any physical danger. But they sure as hell have come to the rescue often enough to make me believe that they have, in a sense, salvaged my dignity on numerous occasions. And that, in my book, is a life-saving endeavor in its own right.

Text: What's the biggest anticlimax in movie history? For me, the biggest cinematic letdown has to be the grand reveal in M. Night Shyamalan's *The Village*. The film, much like the director's other ventures, traffics in the currency of suspense; the subtle build-up, the carefully laid breadcrumbs, the unnerving score designed to keep you on the edge of your seat. You anticipate, for the better part of the film, some horrifying creature lurking in the woods, a menacing presence that threatens the safety of the insular village. The villagers, we learn, have a pact with these creatures, a desperate bargain they uphold through rituals and fear. The film's trailers and marketing campaigns were masterful in their obfuscation, hinting at a supernatural thriller while keeping the true nature of the threat shrouded in mystery. And then, the reveal. The "creatures" aren't monsters, not supernatural beings from some dark realm, but rather…villagers in cloaks. They were an elaborate hoax, a carefully orchestrated deception meant to protect the village from the outside world. It wasn't just a twist; it was a narrative collapse, a deflation of tension so complete that the audience was left reeling. The film, up to that point, had played with the tropes of horror and suspense, but the reveal itself was more akin to a Scooby-Doo episode, a narrative trick lacking the thematic depth and the psychological resonance that Shyamalan often strives for. The film was beautifully shot, with a score that was undeniably effective - but the resolution felt cheap and unsatisfying. All the carefully constructed tension, all the build-up, all the whispers and anxieties of the villagers, reduced to a gimmick. It's not just the plot twist, but how it invalidated the film’s already-established framework. It's like spending a fortune on fireworks only to have them fizzle out mid-air. This single, underwhelming twist overshadowed everything that preceded it, turning a potentially great film into a cautionary tale of thematic and narrative miscalculation. Not to mention, the sheer eye-rolling incredulity of the reveal, it just made you want to shout, 'Are you serious?!'.

Text: As a teacher, have you ever been accused of something? As a teacher, have you ever been accused of something?  I’ve never held the title of educator in any formal capacity. I’m more of a student of life, forever learning, perpetually curious. My classroom is the world, and my lessons often come disguised as observations, experiences, and the occasional bout of introspection. Therefore, I haven't faced the brunt of accusations that come with the territory of being a teacher. But, as an avid observer of the human condition, the subject matter of accusations, be they just or unjust, has always piqued my interest. Specifically, the sheer audacity and the intricate dance of blame that accompany them.  One of the most fascinating, yet infuriating, situations I've ever observed unfolded with a close family friend, a woman named Beatrice. She’s a primary school teacher of twenty plus years, and the type of person who genuinely cares for her students. One day, she was accused by a parent of favouritism; supposedly, her son wasn’t getting the same attention as other children in class. Beatrice, ever the optimist, tried to calmly explain her teaching methods, but the parent was relentless. The accusations, fueled by a mixture of insecurity and a dash of entitlement, escalated quickly. They went from not-so-subtle passive-aggressiveness to outright hostility. It was a masterclass in how baseless accusations can be hurled, a clear example of how the accuser, in their own minds, had already declared their 'truth' and would not bend to contrary evidence or reasoned arguments. It was an ugly situation that, unfortunately, many teachers are subject to from time to time.  The incident underscored a few important points: The power of perception, how easily good intentions can be misconstrued, and the exhausting reality that you can't please everyone.

Text: What things do people say that make you roll your eyes? It’s funny, isn’t it? How some phrases, repeated ad nauseam, can just instantly trigger that involuntary eye roll. I'm probably guilty of saying some myself, at times, but the ones that really get under my skin are the ones that ooze either passive-aggressive condescension or unearned self-importance. Like when someone feigns concern by saying "Are you sure?" after you’ve made a clear decision, implying that you're clearly a bumbling idiot who needs their implicit guidance. Or, when someone, usually someone with a modicum of privilege, launches into, “Well, *I* would never…” as if their personal preferences are some universal standard of morality or propriety.  Then there are the overused clichés, particularly those that operate as empty platitudes, designed to shut down any actual discussion: “Everything happens for a reason". Really? Is that supposed to offer some consolation when someone dear to you dies tragically? Or how about, "It is what it is?" Yes, Captain Obvious, I’m well aware of the immutable nature of reality, but perhaps I was angling for some genuine advice or empathy. Also, I can't stand it when people declare, "I just want to be happy!" as if happiness is some pre-ordained state achievable with a mere declaration. Sorry, pal, but life is a messy, chaotic, inconsistent rollercoaster ride, not some effortless pursuit of bliss.  But the ultimate eye-roll inducer? The phrase, “I could care less.” It’s always misused. What people actually *mean* to say is "I *couldn't* care less", but yet they use it incorrectly, thus proving, in itself, the very sentiment. The amount of times I have had to bite my tongue as someone utters such a statement is infuriating. It’s also a perfect illustration of the way inane, vapid language can degrade and corrupt the English language, one poorly structured sentence at a time.

Text: At what age did you stop enjoying YA fiction? That’s a loaded question, innit? The sort that has me contemplating the very nature of time, memory, and the elusive concept of “enjoyment” itself. If I'm being honest, I've never been a devout follower of Young Adult fiction. I have never been on that bandwagon. There was a time when I thought I was, you know. I’d read a few books that fell vaguely within the genre, like *The Hunger Games* or a handful of John Green's novels, figuring they were the literary equivalent of fast food – quick, easy, and vaguely satisfying while you’re consuming it. But just like cheap take-out, they didn’t stick with me. They didn't leave a lasting taste in my mouth. They didn’t provide the nourishment for my literary cravings. My true literary loves all reside in much loftier realms. Now don’t get me wrong; I’m not knocking the genre entirely. YA fiction does serve a purpose. It introduces teenagers to the world of reading. It gives them something to connect with. It often tackles important themes in a format that's easily digestible. However, the tropes, the melodramatic romance, the all-too-convenient plot devices… they get old, quick. They start to grate on the nerves. Ultimately, it’s an invitation for me to groan, roll my eyes, and toss the book aside in favor of something with a bit more substance, something that actually makes me think. So, at what age did I stop enjoying YA fiction? I'd say I never really did, to begin with.

Text: What show / movie had no right to be as good as it was? “The Boys” is the show that immediately springs to mind. When I first heard about it, I thought it was going to be another generic superhero caricature, replete with the usual tired tropes and clichés. Yet another attempt to squeeze more blood (pun intended) out of the superhero stone. I was so certain that I was correct in my assessment that I was convinced I would watch it for maybe half an episode. I watched the first three episodes in one sitting. The show is, in short, excellent. I would even go as far as to say it is one of the best shows I have ever seen. And I don't just mean in the superhero genre. What sets “The Boys” apart from the pantheon of run-of-the-mill superhero shows and movies is its unflinching take down of the superhero industrial complex. While other superhero shows are content with using vague ideas of moral ambiguity, “The Boys” treats the subject with a dark sardonic twist. The show seems to revel in the absurdity of the world it has created by displaying the ugly side of the superhero persona. You have the heroes, the mega-corporations that own heroes, the PR teams that clean up the heroes' messes, the fans who are obsessed with the heroes, and yes, even the villains who seem to be almost as reprehensible as the good guys. The show even takes the time to satirize the darker facets of the modern world. They don't just play with these elements. They hold a mirror up to society and force you to laugh at all the ugliness. And I wasn't expecting any of that. I was expecting another show that was trying to be “woke” with shallow social commentary or a movie where the hero suddenly discovers that someone they knew was secretly evil. What I got instead was something smart, insightful, and frequently hilarious. The show's violence is gratuitous, sure, but the show also has heart. So much heart, in fact, that you can forgive the violence. The characters' relationships with each other are well-written, and the acting is top-notch. I would suggest anyone who is interested in an subversive superhero show to give it a watch.

Text: What is the most obnoxious thing you have seen someone do at the grocery store? I've witnessed a litany of offenses in the hallowed aisles of the grocery store, each a minor affront to my sensibilities. But one particular incident rises above the rest in terms of pure, unadulterated obnoxiousness. It happened a few years ago – feels like a lifetime, actually – and I still shudder when I think about it. I was patiently waiting in the express checkout line, the one with the "10 items or less" sign. As usual, it was clogged with slow-moving customers, each meticulously examining their produce before finally handing it over to the cashier. A veritable symphony of sighs, and the gentle *beep* of the scanner at its regular pace. Suddenly, a woman, perhaps in her late fifties, breezed in, pushing a cart overflowing with items. And I mean *overflowing*. It was a genuine mountain of groceries. She glanced at the sign, then looked at the cashier, gave a dismissive chuckle, and proceeded to unload her haul onto the conveyor belt. The cashier, bless her soul, looked utterly defeated, but knew she couldn't say anything. The woman then started acting like she was the star of her own personal show. Each item received a dramatic pause, a scrutinising examination, presumably for any sign of imperfection. The line behind me began to grow. Murmurs of disapproval started to bubble up from the assembled masses of shoppers. A young mother with a screaming toddler gave the woman a withering look. But did she care? Not a damn bit. She was too engrossed in her own self-importance to notice the petty turmoil she caused. The sheer audacity of her actions was enough to send me into a state of silent, seething rage. It was a display of flagrant disregard for the rules, for common decency, and for everyone else's time. It was, in a word, obnoxious. The woman eventually finished, paid, and exited the store, leaving a trail of frustrated shoppers in her wake. I, meanwhile, was left with a lingering feeling of bewilderment. Where did she get the nerve? What made her think her time was more valuable than everyone else's? It remains a mystery that continues to perplex me. And that, dear readers, is the most obnoxious thing I've ever seen at the grocery store.

Text: If all animals were horse-sized, which would be the most majestic to ride into battle? This is difficult to answer because the animal to mount into battle would depend on the role it has to play. If it's a slow-moving, highly armoured, tank-like role, then perhaps a horse-sized tortoise or armadillo. If the role is to ferry supplies and troops across land regardless of how dangerous, then a horse-sized elephant. However, the animal who looks the most visually majestic to ride into battle, in my humble opinion, would have to be a horse-sized lion. Imagine the sight of such a creature clad in shining armour, its mane billowing in the wind, its roars echoing across the battlefield, its massive claws tearing through enemy ranks. A lion, the king of the jungle, amplified to the scale of a horse, is the definition of raw power and untamed elegance. The mere sight of it would be enough to demoralize any enemy. A lion exudes an aura of dominance, a primal ferocity that's unmatched in the animal kingdom. Its sleek, powerful form, the glint in its predatory eyes, the sheer presence it commands – these are the elements of true majesty. As it charges towards the enemy, its muscles rippling beneath its fearsome visage, it would be a sight to behold. Text: What is the lamest “benefit” you’ve been offered by an employer? I have worked a fair share of odd jobs in my life, mainly to fund my tuition fees or to simply find some extra pocket money on the side. As such I’ve encountered companies offering a plethora of “benefits” to lure me on board. I’ve seen it all: the free coffee, the ping pong tables, the pool tables, the Friday afternoon beer sessions, the monthly all you can eat breakfasts and the occasional company barbeque. Most of the time I would laugh about the ridiculousness of it all and then promptly refuse the job offers. However there was this one instance that takes the cake. I was in the penultimate year of my degree and I needed some real income to fund a rather crucial thesis. The job advertised was for a cashier at a local supermarket chain at a starting salary of $3000 a month. I thought that was a bit too low since I was coming away with $2000 a month at the time but I went anyway. Upon arriving I was surprised as to the scale of the place. It was HUGE, filled with almost every product you can imagine. This was the biggest supermarket on the island. It was filled to the brim with customers. The sheer amount of people in the shop was unbelievable. I was slightly intimidated. After all, I had only worked behind the till a handful of times. I had a brief interview with a middle aged lady who was the HR manager. She was friendly and enthusiastic as she explained the functions of the role. I was even more surprised when she told me the salary was actually $3500 a month. An additional $500 was a sizeable boost. The catch? As she explained, you would have to “earn” it as you go. She elaborated in detail the performance metrics. The more you perform, the higher the salary. As she ended her explanation, she looked in the most pleasant way possible and told me about the additional benefits. “We offer a flexible schedule which is determined by your performance! You can tell us whether you would like to work a full day or half a day.” I sat upright to pay closer attention. My ears perked up. I thought to myself, “Wow, that’s convenient!” The HR manager then continued: “And, most importantly you get a staff discount on ALL products in the shop! So if you are buying some groceries….you can receive a steep discount.” I paused. I scratched my head. I knew what was coming. “The maximum discount?”, I asked. “10%”, she replied with an eager smile. I laughed. I told her that I would call her. The biggest supermarket on the island was trying to entice me with a measly 10% discount on its shelves. I told her my current job offered a 20% discount. I rejected the offer and felt a little sorry for her and walked away.

"What is the lamest \u201cbenefit\u201d you\u2019ve been offered by an employer? I have worked a fair share of odd jobs in my life, mainly to fund my tuition fees or to simply find some extra pocket money on the side. As such I\u2019ve encountered companies offering a plethora of \u201cbenefits\u201d to lure me on board. I\u2019ve seen it all: the free coffee, the ping pong tables, the pool tables, the Friday afternoon beer sessions, the monthly all you can eat breakfasts and the occasional company barbeque. Most of the time I would laugh about the ridiculousness of it all and then promptly refuse the job offers. However there was this one instance that takes the cake. I was in the penultimate year of my degree and I needed some real income to fund a rather crucial thesis. The job advertised was for a cashier at a local supermarket chain at a starting salary of $3000 a month. I thought that was a bit too low since I was coming away with $2000 a month at the time but I went anyway. Upon arriving I was surprised as to the scale of the place. It was HUGE, filled with almost every product you can imagine. This was the biggest supermarket on the island. It was filled to the brim with customers. The sheer amount of people in the shop was unbelievable. I was slightly intimidated. After all, I had only worked behind the till a handful of times. I had a brief interview with a middle aged lady who was the HR manager. She was friendly and enthusiastic as she explained the functions of the role. I was even more surprised when she told me the salary was actually $3500 a month. An additional $500 was a sizeable boost. The catch? As she explained, you would have to \u201cearn\u201d it as you go. She elaborated in detail the performance metrics. The more you perform, the higher the salary. As she ended her explanation, she looked in the most pleasant way possible and told me about the additional benefits. \u201cWe offer a flexible schedule which is determined by your performance! You can tell us whether you would like to work a full day or half a day.\u201d I sat upright to pay closer attention. My ears perked up. I thought to myself, \u201cWow, that\u2019s convenient!\u201d The HR manager then continued: \u201cAnd, most importantly you get a staff discount on ALL products in the shop! So if you are buying some groceries\u2026.you can receive a steep discount.\u201d I paused. I scratched my head. I knew what was coming. \u201cThe maximum discount?\u201d, I asked. \u201c10%\u201d, she replied with an eager smile. I laughed. I told her that I would call her. The biggest supermarket on the island was trying to entice me with a measly 10% discount on its shelves. I told her my current job offered a 20% discount. I rejected the offer and felt a little sorry for her and walked away.  "}], "editorDocumentId": null}

Text: What is the lowest probability event you have personally witnessed? "Unbelievable," I thought to myself, "Can this really be happening again?" A sense of impending doom washed over me. I could feel a wave of resignation creeping in. The probability of this event -- this **exact** event -- happening again was astronomically small. Forget about winning the lottery, this was in another realm of impossibility. I was flummoxed. I could not believe my eyes. Having already once experienced Gandhi's incessant chatter for six whole hours during the course of a cross country trip, the prospect of enduring a second experience of such a cataclysmic ordeal was too much to bear. As if the universe had a vendetta against my sanity. I was resigned to my fate. The irony of it all was almost comical. Of all the people in the world, and across two vastly different locations (Dominica and back in Trinidad), I had, once again, landed myself beside my acquaintance and tormentor. This time in a different country, on a different journey and on a different bus. It felt almost like a cruel joke. A cosmic prank orchestrated by some unseen force. I struggled to maintain a modicum of composure and, bracing myself. The monotonous drone began.

Text: What's the most ridiculous thing a coworker told on you to your boss for? I once worked with a woman I shall call "The Oracle". The Oracle was of advanced age, a fixture in the department, and possessed a peculiar blend of wisdom and… let’s say, "opinionatedness." She was the kind of person who knew *everything* about everyone, and wasn't shy about dispensing that knowledge – whether it was wanted or not. The office rumour mill, in the form of The Oracle, was in perpetual operation, and it’s safe to say, everyone was on it, myself very much included. My transgression? Apparently, I possessed the audacity to enjoy a lengthy lunch break.  It started innocently enough. I was on a very tight deadline, and since I was working on a very demanding project I decided to take an extended lunch break to clear my head. I was probably two or three hours late at that point. I went for a long walk, bought a sandwich, and generally tried to de-stress. I came back feeling refreshed and ready to tackle the mountain of work ahead. Unfortunately for me, The Oracle was on duty that day. Upon seeing me return, she summoned me to her desk with a look of grave importance.  “You were gone for three hours,” she stated, her voice a low rumble of disapproval. “The boss is not going to like this. You are being very disrespectful to your superiors and to your coworkers. Many people have to work and work, and you just go gallivanting for three hours.” At that moment it struck me that perhaps The Oracle was secretly hoping for an opportunity to get promoted due to her dedication to keeping the employees in check.  I explained my rationale – the deadline, the project, the need to clear my head. She listened, her expression unyielding, then simply shook her head and issued a stern, "I’m telling the boss." And so, she did. The next day, I was called into my supervisor's office. I anticipated a stern talking-to, maybe even a reprimand. What I wasn’t expecting was the sheer absurdity of the situation. The supervisor, a man known for his laid-back style, was trying his best to suppress a grin.  “So,” he said, leaning back in his chair, “I hear you enjoy extended lunch breaks.” I explained myself again, feeling a blush creep up my neck. He listened, nodding slowly, then made a surprising statement. “Well, The Oracle told me that perhaps you should be fired. But that would not be realistic. The company needs you.” Thus, I somehow escaped The Oracle's wrath. It was, without question, the most ridiculous thing a coworker has ever told on me. The incident cemented her legendary status within the office. And on days she was absent the office experienced complete chaos.
